title: OmniCVR: A Benchmark for Omni-Composed Video Retrieval with Vision, Audio, and Text
claim: The benchmark spans distinct query types, each pairing a source video, a modification instruction, and a target video, that stress different modalities.
layout: 3 side-by-side colored panels; each stacks source video, text, then target video
description: Three rounded panels sit side by side, titled Audio-Centric (lavender), Integrated (blue) and Vision-Centric (green). Each panel stacks a source video, a modification instruction and a target video. The source and target videos are strips of three frames, each with a small audio waveform icon at the right. The Audio-Centric panel shows an interviewed man in a blue shirt, and its text asks for a shift from past recollection to future-looking discussion. The Integrated panel shows a disc golf scene on a lawn, with edits to shirt color, dog positions and audio. The Vision-Centric panel shows a graffiti artist in red painting a wall, with the artwork moving from an outline to a finished piece. Bold 'Modification Text:' labels lead each instruction. The eye goes first to the photos, then to the dense text blocks.
caption: Overview of the OmniCVR Benchmark.
abstract: Composed video retrieval presents a complex challenge: retrieving a target video based on a source video and a textual modification instruction. This task demands fine-grained reasoning over multimodal transformations. However, existing benchmarks predominantly focus on vision–text alignment, largely overlooking the rich semantic signals embedded in audio—such as speech, music, and environmental sounds—which are often decisive for comprehensive video understanding. To bridge this gap, we introduce OmniCVR , a large-scale benchmark for omni-composed video retrieval that establishes vision, audio, and text as first-class modalities. OmniCVR is constructed via a scalable, automated pipeline integrating content-aware segmentation, omni-modal annotation, and a rigorous dual-validation protocol involving both large language models and human experts. The benchmark comprises vision-centric, audio-centric, and integrated queries, with the latter forming the majority to accurately reflect real-world multimodal complexity. Furthermore, we propose AudioVLM2Vec , an audio-aware extension of VLM2Vec. By incorporating explicit audio semantics, AudioVLM2Vec achieves state-of-the-art performance, highlighting fundamental limitations in the audio reasoning capabilities of current multimodal retrieval systems.
